        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow locally.  
I’ll provide the exact file contents you should create, and then the Git commands you’ll need to stage, commit and push them back to the remote.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH access, use HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file called `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```Dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why node:18-alpine?*  
> Alpine images are small and fast; Node 18 is the LTS version at the time of writing.  
> Adjust the base image if your app requires a different Node version.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory called `k8s` (or use an existing one) and inside it create a file called `deployment.yaml` with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **Image name** – Replace `nodejs-welcome:latest` with the full image reference you’ll push to (e.g. `docker.io/<your-dockerhub-username>/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  
> **Replicas** – Two pods are a good starting point; adjust as needed.  
> **Service type** – `ClusterIP` keeps the service internal to the cluster. Change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and inside it create a file called `build-and-push.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'   # match the Docker base image

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets** – In the GitHub repo settings → Secrets → Actions, add:
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub personal access token (recommended over password)

> **Why this workflow?**  
> • Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> • Installs dependencies, runs tests, builds the Docker image, and pushes it to Docker Hub.  

> **Adjustments** – If you’re using another registry (GitHub Packages, ECR, GCR, …), change the login action and the `tags:` line accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run (you’ll see it under the “Actions” tab).  
> Once it succeeds, your Docker image will be available in Docker Hub and ready to deploy with `kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml`.

---

### Quick sanity checks

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `docker build -t nodejs-welcome:latest .` | Builds the image locally |
| `docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:latest` | Runs the container locally |
| `kubectl get pods` | Lists running pods |
| `kubectl get svc` | Shows the service IP/port |

---

That’s it!  
Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or service type to suit your production environment. Happy deploying!
